title: Fiona the Hippo Died After Eating a Hat. But How Does a Hat Kill a Hippo?
gist: Fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo's nine-year-old hippo, died after swallowing a knit hat that a fan launched into her enclosure; veterinary experts explain that a blockage in a 100-plus-foot intestinal tract can cause swelling or twisting, tissue death, rupture and toxic shock. Surgery was ruled out because hippos respond unpredictably to anesthesia and their size makes ventilation and positioning extremely risky, so the zoo tried non-surgical measures that ultimately failed.

themes.theme: How an intestinal blockage kills a hippo

insights.claim: A hippo's intestinal tract is estimated at over 100 feet long, including more than 70 feet of small intestine, versus about 25 feet in humans; in a healthy hippo liquids pass in about 12 hours and food in two to three days, so a swallowed object would likely have passed within five days if it was going to.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
entities: North Carolina State University College of Veterinary Medicine
insights.so_what: Context for why foreign-body ingestion is a high-stakes animal-welfare and liability risk for zoos.

insights.claim: A stuck foreign object in a hippo can kill via two routes: swelling and pressure that cut off circulation, or intestines twisting around a heavy object; either leads to tissue death, leaking or rupture, bacterial toxins in the bloodstream, organ inflammation and failure.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Explains the likely mechanism pending a post-mortem; non-degradable or rigid materials such as polyester or plastic are far more dangerous than cotton.

insights.claim: Hippos respond unpredictably and irregularly to sedation and anesthesia and can die from standard medications used on elephants and rhinos, making major surgery on a hippo very risky.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: A known gap in large-animal veterinary medicine; specialized anesthesia protocols for hippos remain poorly understood.
insights.quote: It is very risky for [hippos], and they can die from the standard medication used on other large animals, like elephants and rhinos, for reasons we don't well understand,
insights.locator: Rebecca Lewison—San Diego State University biology professor

insights.claim: Major surgery on a 2,500-plus-pound hippo would require far more anesthesia than bloodwork, an oversized ventilator, hoists or forklifts for positioning, and long periods immobile under its own body weight that impair oxygen circulation, with dehydration further raising risk.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: Illustrates the practical limits of veterinary intervention for megafauna even at well-resourced zoos.
insights.quote: You would have to have a hoist, a forklift or something, to pick them up to put them on either a pad or on a table,

insights.claim: The Cincinnati Zoo said a child's hat hit a ceiling fan and was launched through a one-foot gap above Fiona's 12-foot viewing window; with surgery ruled out, staff used ultrasound, fluids, an enema, medication, a nine-foot scope borrowed from Columbus Zoo and a vibration plate from a horse farm before she died.
insights.speaker: Caroline Haskins
insights.so_what: An enclosure design gap allowed a fatal incident, which may prompt zoos to review barrier design for visitor-thrown objects.
